title: Defensive Parameter Cloning to Evade Lifetimes
pattern: An API systematically accepts parameters by reference and calls `.to_string()`, `.to_owned()`, or `.clone()` internally to populate struct fields, in order to avoid putting lifetime parameters on the struct.
why_bad: This is the inverse of the first pattern. To keep the API signature superficially "clean" (free of `'a` annotations), it forces a silent allocation cost on every call, even if the caller already owns a `String` and could have moved it. It strips the caller of control over allocation, making high-frequency loops or bulk operations highly inefficient.
detection: Public constructors or builder methods that accept reference types (`&str`, `&[T]`) and immediately call `.clone()`, `.to_string()`, or `.to_vec()` on them to initialize struct fields, without providing an alternative owned consuming constructor.
counterexample: Accepting references is valid when the struct must hold a borrow and lifetimes are intended to restrict its scope, or when the cost of cloning is demonstrably negligible and ergonomics is the overriding concern. Mark `Context-dependent`.
